You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this - finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool - does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only - your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

1 # bat 2 3

4 A cat(1) clone with syntax highlighting and Git integration. 5

6 7 ## Key Features 8 9 ### Syntax highlighting 10 11 `bat` supports syntax highlighting for a large number of programming and markup languages. 12 13 ### Git integration 14 15 `bat` communicates with `git` to show modifications with respect to the index. 16 17 ### Show non-printable characters 18 19 You can use the `-A`/`--show-all` option to show and highlight non-printable characters. 20 21 ### Automatic paging 22 23 By default, `bat` pipes its own output to a pager (e.g. `less`) if the output is too large for one screen. 24 If you would rather `bat` work like `cat` all the time (never page output), you can set `--paging=never` as an option, either on the command line or in your configuration file. 25 If you intend to alias `cat` to `bat` in your shell configuration, you can use `alias cat='bat --paging=never'` to preserve the default behavior. 26 27 #### File concatenation 28 29 Even with a pager set, you can still use `bat` to concatenate files. 30 Whenever `bat` detects a non-interactive terminal (i.e. when you pipe into another process or into a file), `bat` will act as a drop-in replacement for `cat` and fall back to printing the plain file contents, regardless of the `--pager` option's value. 31 32 ## How to use 33 34 Display a single file on the terminal: 35 36 ```bash 37 bat README.md 38 ``` 39 40 Display multiple files at once: 41 42 ```bash 43 bat src/*.rs 44 ``` 45 46 Read from stdin, determine the syntax automatically: 47 48 ```bash 49 curl -s https://sh.rustup.rs | bat 50 ``` 51 52 Read from stdin, specify the language explicitly: 53 54 ```bash 55 yaml2json .travis.yml | json_pp | bat -l json 56 ``` 57 58 Show and highlight non-printable characters: 59 60 ```bash 61 bat -A /etc/hosts 62 ``` 63 64 Use it as a `cat` replacement: 65 66 ```bash 67 bat > note.md # quickly create a new file 68 69 bat header.md content.md footer.md > document.md 70 71 bat -n main.rs # show line numbers (only) 72 73 bat f - g # output 'f', then stdin, then 'g'. 74 ``` 75 76 ### Integration with other tools 77 78 #### `fzf` 79 80 You can use `bat` as a previewer for `fzf`: 81 82 ```bash 83 fzf --preview "bat --color=always --style=numbers --line-range=:500 {}" 84 ``` 85 86 #### `find` or `fd` 87 88 Preview all search results with `bat`: 89 90 ```bash 91 find … -exec bat {} + 92 fd … -X bat 93 ``` 94 95 #### `ripgrep` 96 97 With `batgrep`, `bat` can be used as the printer for `ripgrep` search results: 98 99 ```bash 100 batgrep needle src/ 101 ``` 102 103 #### `tail -f` 104 105 `bat` can be combined with `tail -f` to continuously monitor a given file with syntax highlighting: 106 107 ```bash 108 tail -f /var/log/pacman.log | bat --paging=never -l log 109 ``` 110 111 #### `git` 112 113 Combine `bat` with `git show` to view an older version of a file with syntax highlighting: 114 115 ```bash 116 git show v0.6.0:src/main.rs | bat -l rs 117 ``` 118 119 #### `git diff` 120 121 Combine `bat` with `git diff` to view lines around code changes: 122 123 ```bash 124 batdiff() { 125 git diff --name-only --relative --diff-filter=d -z | xargs -0 bat --diff 126 } 127 ``` 128 129 #### `xclip` 130 131 Pipe the output into `xclip` to copy file contents: 132 133 ```bash 134 bat main.cpp | xclip 135 ``` 136 137 `bat` will detect that the output is being redirected and print the plain file contents. 138 139 #### `man` 140 141 `bat` can be used as a colorizing pager for `man`: 142 143 ```bash 144 export MANPAGER="bat -plman" 145 man 2 select 146 ``` 147 148 #### Highlighting `--help` messages 149 150 You can use `bat` to colorize help text: 151 152 ```bash 153 cp --help | bat -plhelp 154 ``` 155 156 Or use a wrapper: 157 158 ```bash 159 alias bathelp='bat --plain --language=help' 160 help() { 161 "$@" --help 2>&1 | bathelp 162 } 163 ``` 164 165 ## Installation 166 167 Download prebuilt binaries from the release page for your platform. 168 169 `bat` is also available through various package managers: 170 171 - Ubuntu/Debian: `sudo apt install bat` 172 - Alpine: `apk add bat` 173 - Arch: `pacman -S bat` 174 - Fedora: `dnf install bat` 175 - Gentoo: `emerge sys-apps/bat` 176 - FreeBSD: `pkg install bat` 177 - OpenBSD: `pkg_add bat` 178 - Nix: `nix-env -i bat` 179 - openSUSE: `zypper install bat` 180 - macOS (Homebrew): `brew install bat` 181 - macOS (MacPorts): `port install bat` 182 - Windows (WinGet): `winget install sharkdp.bat` 183 - Windows (Chocolatey): `choco install bat` 184 - Windows (Scoop): `scoop install bat` 185 186 ## Customization 187 188 ### Highlighting theme 189 190 Use `bat --list-themes` to get a list of all available themes for syntax highlighting. 191 192 To select a theme, use the `--theme` option: 193 194 ```bash 195 bat --theme=TwoDark myfile.txt 196 ``` 197 198 Or set the `BAT_THEME` environment variable: 199 200 ```bash 201 export BAT_THEME="TwoDark" 202 ``` 203 204 `bat` automatically picks a fitting theme depending on your terminal's background color. You can use the `--theme-dark` / `--theme-light` options or the `BAT_THEME_DARK` / `BAT_THEME_LIGHT` environment variables to customize the themes used. 205 206 ### Output style 207 208 Use the `--style` option to control the appearance of `bat`'s output: 209 210 ```bash 211 bat --style=numbers,changes myfile.txt 212 ``` 213 214 Set the `BAT_STYLE` environment variable to make these changes permanent. 215 216 ### Decorations 217 218 By default, `bat` only shows decorations when outputting to an interactive terminal. Control this with the `--decorations` option: 219 220 ```bash 221 bat --decorations=always myfile.txt # always show decorations 222 bat --decorations=never myfile.txt # never show decorations 223 ``` 224 225 ### Using a different pager 226 227 `bat` uses the pager specified in the `PAGER` environment variable. If not set, `less` is used by default. You can also use bat's built-in pager with `--pager=builtin`. 228 229 To use a different pager: 230 231 ```bash 232 export BAT_PAGER="less -RF" 233 ``` 234 235 ### Configuration file 236 237 `bat` can be customized with a configuration file. To get the default path: 238 239 ```bash 240 bat --config-file 241 ``` 242 243 Generate a default configuration file: 244 245 ```bash 246 bat --generate-config-file 247 ``` 248 249 The configuration file is a simple list of command line arguments. Example: 250 251 ```bash 252 # Set the theme 253 --theme="TwoDark" 254 255 # Show line numbers, Git modifications and file header 256 --style="numbers,changes,header" 257 258 # Use C++ syntax for Arduino .ino files 259 --map-syntax "*.ino:C++" 260 ``` 261 262 ## Command-line options 263 264 For a full list of options, run: 265 266 ```bash 267 bat --help 268 ``` 269 270 ## Project goals 271 272 `bat` tries to achieve the following goals: 273 274 - Provide beautiful, advanced syntax highlighting 275 - Integrate with Git to show file modifications 276 - Be a drop-in replacement for (POSIX) `cat` 277 - Offer a user-friendly command-line interface 278 279 ## License 280 281 Copyright (c) 2018-2025 bat-developers 282 283 `bat` is made available under the terms of either the MIT License or the Apache License 2.0, at your option. 284 285 See the LICENSE-APACHE and LICENSE-MIT files for license details.
